title: neolithic greenstone axe found beside tuscan thermal spring
dek: an unused polished axe travelled hundreds of kilometres to rest beside hot waters
body: archaeologists excavating an ancient thermal spring in Tuscany have discovered an intact neolithic greenstone axe that originated hundreds of kilometres away in the western alps. the polished axe was discovered inside a large travertine cave at the terme di sorano in the province of grosseto, where archaeological evidence indicates people were visiting a thermal spring by the middle of the 5th millennium bc. microscopic analysis has identified the stone as eclogite, a distinctive green rock almost certainly originating in the western alps.

despite travelling hundreds of kilometres before reaching tuscan, the axe appears never to have been used. its cutting edge remains intact and shows no evidence of wear, leading archaeologists to suggest that the object may have been deposited near the thermal waters for symbolic or ritual purposes. the sorano axe is small, carefully polished and retains its original sharp cutting edge. the absence of wear suggests it was not manufactured for everyday use. its distant geological origin is also significant. eclogite was obtained from the western alps, both from high-altitude sources and from river and glacial deposits, meaning the object or its raw material travelled hundreds of kilometres before reaching central italy.

excavation director stefano giuntoli believes the exceptional preservation of the axe, combined with its valuable material and archaeological context, supports an interpretation as a symbolic object. across neolithic europe, prestigious polished stone axes have been discovered in high-status burials and at places interpreted as ritual sites. some were deliberately deposited in landscapes associated with water, including springs, wetlands and waterfalls. the discovery of an unused example beside a thermal spring emerging directly from the rock is therefore compatible with deliberate ritual deposition, although the precise circumstances in which the sorano axe entered the cave remain unknown.

relatively few pottery and stone artefacts have been recovered compared with the size of the excavated area. researchers believe this may indicate that the cave was not a permanent settlement, but instead served a specialised purpose connected with the thermal spring. the pottery consists primarily of fragments from vessels made using coarse and semi-refined fabrics, some decorated with relief designs. stone artefacts include flint and jasper cores and waste produced during tool manufacture.

animal remains recovered from the site may provide further evidence about activities taking place around the spring. domestic species dominate the assemblage, particularly cattle, pigs and sheep, while horse-family animals and canids are also represented. wild species, including deer, roe deer and fox, occur in smaller numbers. several cattle were young or subadult when they died. researchers have not yet established whether the animal remains resulted from ritual practices or more routine activities.

the excavations are being carried out under a concession from italy’s ministry of culture, and specialists are studying the site’s archaeological, geological, environmental and animal remains. three-dimensional recording and photogrammetry are also being used to document the cave and its structures. now researchers are trying to find out what purpose the stone constructions served and when they were built, as well as how artefacts and animal remains fit in with activities around the thermal spring.

for now, the evidence from sorano is that people were using the hot waters there in neolithic times, and the pristine alpine axe shows further evidence that the spring may have had more than utilitarian significance.
doesnt_show: why the axe was deposited and who deposited it remain unclear
settle: further excavation and dating of the stone structures and animal remains will clarify the ritual context
